question: During which phase of the cell cycle does a cell make a copy of its DNA?
explanation: You got this! The S phase (synthesis phase) is specifically when the cell replicates its genetic material before dividing. Think 'S' for 'Synthesis' or 'Copying'! [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h1)

question: What is the main job of checkpoints in the normal cell cycle?

options.A: To stop division if DNA damage is found
options.C: To provide energy for the cell to split
options.D: To turn active cells into resting cells

explanation: Great try! Cell checkpoints act like security guards—they inspect the cell and halt the cycle if anything looks damaged, keeping the body safe. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h1)

question: When one mature cell type changes into another mature cell type due to ongoing irritation, what is it called?
explanation: Spot on! Metaplasia is like a cellular makeover; cells switch to a tougher type to better handle chronic stress, such as smoke irritation in the airways. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h2)

question: A lab report describes tissue with disordered growth and cells of varying shapes and sizes. Which term describes this?
explanation: Well done! Dysplasia means disordered growth where cells lose their normal shape and organization—often an early warning sign that nurses watch closely. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h2)

question: What do we call the process where cancer cells break away and spread through the blood or lymph to other parts of the body?
explanation: You're doing great! Metastasis happens when malignant cells travel via blood or lymph to set up secondary growths in distant organs. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h3)

question: Which of these is a typical feature of a benign (non-cancerous) tumor?
explanation: Correct! Benign tumors usually stay put inside a neat fibrous capsule, meaning they don't invade nearby tissues or spread around. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h3)

question: What are the two big features that define all stem cells?
explanation: Spot on! Stem cells are amazing because they can both make copies of themselves (self-renewal) and turn into specialized cells (potency). [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h4)

question: Why is cellular differentiation so important for the human body?

options.A: It ensures that all cells in the body remain identical
options.B: It stops normal cells from resting
options.C: It allows basic cells to mature into specific functional cells
options.D: It keeps the immune system calm

explanation: Brilliant! Differentiation is how a simple stem cell becomes a specialized muscle, nerve, or blood cell to do specific jobs in the body. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h4)

question: What is the main underlying cause of uncontrolled cell growth in cancer?

options.B: Permanent resting state in the cells
options.C: A total lack of cellular respiration

explanation: You've got it! Cancer starts when genetic errors build up over time, breaking the normal rules that tell cells when to stop growing. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h5)

question: Why do advanced tumors often become resistant to medical treatments like chemotherapy?

options.A: The body's immune system destroys the medication before it reaches the tumor
options.B: Chemotherapy drugs turn normal cells into malignant cancer cells
options.C: Genetic diversity creates varied cell populations with different drug resistance traits
options.D: Tumor cells develop a protective bone shell that blocks all medications

explanation: As mutations accumulate, cancer cells become diverse; while some cells die from treatment, resistant clones survive and multiply. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h5)

question: What is the normal, healthy job of proto-oncogenes in our bodies?

options.C: Promoting normal cell growth and division

explanation: Spot on! Proto-oncogenes are normal, helpful genes that tell cells when it's time to grow and repair tissues. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h6)

question: What happens when a tumor suppressor gene experiences a loss-of-function mutation?

options.A: The cell immediately transforms into a benign fibrous cyst
options.B: The cell loses its molecular brakes and divides uncontrollably
options.C: The cell creates an outer capsule to prevent metastasis
options.D: Normal cellular division stops permanently in the G0 phase

explanation: Tumor suppressor genes normally slow down cell growth; losing them removes these protective brakes, allowing rapid tumor growth. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h6)

question: What is the main role of apoptosis in the body?

options.A: Removing damaged or unneeded cells in a neat, orderly way
options.B: Causing sudden inflammation after an injury

explanation: Correct! Apoptosis is the body's clean-up process—it gently removes old or damaged cells without causing messy inflammation. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h7)

question: How do cancer cells frequently manipulate apoptosis to survive and multiply?

options.A: They trigger excessive external death receptor signals
options.B: They replace damaged mitochondria with healthy ones
options.C: They mutate regulatory genes to evade programmed cell death
options.D: They speed up the intrinsic pathway to destroy healthy tissue

explanation: Cancer cells often survive by disabling the normal suicide signals that would normally force a damaged cell to die. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h7)

question: Why do traditional chemotherapy drugs commonly cause side effects like hair loss and mucosal sores?

options.A: They cause the patient's immune system to attack hair follicles
options.B: They attack all rapidly dividing cells, both cancerous and normal
options.C: They block the formation of protective fibrous tumor capsules
options.D: They stimulate normal cells to enter permanent resting phases

explanation: Traditional chemotherapy targets rapidly dividing cells, which inadvertently damages healthy tissues with high turnover like hair follicles and gut linings. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h8)

question: A patient on chemotherapy has a very low white blood cell count. What is the top nursing priority?

options.B: Giving medication to help hair grow back
options.C: Preparing the patient for emergency surgery
options.D: Monitoring closely for signs of infection

explanation: Brilliant nursing judgment! Low white blood cells (neutropenia) mean the immune system is weak, so watching for and preventing infection is your #1 priority. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h8)
